explanations.answer: Gather up their belongings from the land
explanations.explanation: That's the order, friend: "Gather up your belongings from this land, you who live under siege." (Jeremiah 10:17) Nobody is told to fight or to build. They're told to pack. I think that's a lot to take in when you're living under siege.

explanations.answer: Rebuild the walls around their city
explanations.explanation: Nice instinct, baker, but nobody picks up a trowel here. The people under siege are told to "Gather up your belongings from this land…" (Jeremiah 10:17) The passage says nothing about walls. It's a packing order, not a building order.

explanations.answer: Open the gates to the enemy army
explanations.explanation: Close, baker, but the gates aren't in this verse. What it says is "Gather up your belongings from this land, you who live under siege." (Jeremiah 10:17) The order is to pack, and that's all it says. Nothing about the gates is in the line.

Yep, and the word is SLING. The LORD says, "Behold, at this time I will sling out the inhabitants of the land…" (Jeremiah 10:18) That's not a gentle walk to the door. It's a word with some force behind it.

This one is true, friend. The LORD says, "Behold, at this time I will sling out the inhabitants of the land and bring distress upon them so that they may be captured." (Jeremiah 10:18) Sling is a strong word, and it's right there in the verse. I'd have doubted it too, honestly.
That's the word. The LORD says He'll "…bring distress upon them so that they may be captured." (Jeremiah 10:18) It's a hard line, and I won't dress it up. The text just says it plainly.
I wish the verse went that way, baker, but it doesn't. The LORD says He'll bring distress on them "…so that they may be captured." (Jeremiah 10:18) Captured is the word the text uses.

Healing is a lovely word, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says He'll bring distress upon them "…so that they may be captured." (Jeremiah 10:18) The wound comes up in the next verse, and there it's still a wound.

explanations.answer: It is my sickness and I must bear it
explanations.explanation: That's it. After the cry of woe, the speaker says, "This is truly my sickness, and I must bear it." (Jeremiah 10:19) No blaming, no dodging. I think that's a heavy thing to say out loud.

explanations.answer: Someone else caused it and must fix it
explanations.explanation: Pointing the finger would be the easy move, friend. But the speaker says, "This is truly my sickness, and I must bear it." (Jeremiah 10:19) Nobody is handed the blame in that line. The speaker takes it on.

explanations.answer: It will heal on its own before long
explanations.explanation: Wouldn't that be nice? The verse doesn't say that, though. The speaker says, "This is truly my sickness, and I must bear it." (Jeremiah 10:19) The word there is bear.

Not quite, friend, and this one is sad. The text says, "My sons have departed from me and are no more." (Jeremiah 10:20) The sons are not close by. So there's nobody standing by to help put the tent back up.

Right, the sons are not around. The text says, "My sons have departed from me and are no more. I have no one left to pitch my tent or set up my curtains." (Jeremiah 10:20) A tent with no one left to raise it. I think this is a heavy one.

Flock it is. "…they have not prospered, and all their flock is scattered." (Jeremiah 10:21) The shepherds don't seek the LORD, and the flock they were supposed to look after is scattered. That's a shepherd's worst day.

Silver's a sensible guess, but the verse talks about sheep, not money. It says, "…they have not prospered, and all their flock is scattered." (Jeremiah 10:21) A shepherd's job is the flock, so the flock is what scatters.

Gold would make a shiny answer, baker, but it's not in the verse. The text says, "…they have not prospered, and all their flock is scattered." (Jeremiah 10:21) These are shepherds, so the word is flock.
North it is. The text says, "Listen! The sound of a report is coming—a great commotion from the land to the north." (Jeremiah 10:22) Good ears, baker.
South sounds reasonable, but the compass says otherwise. The verse says the great commotion comes "…from the land to the north." (Jeremiah 10:22) Check your map, friend.
The sea is a fun pick, but the passage doesn't mention one. It says the commotion is "…from the land to the north." (Jeremiah 10:22) That's a direction and it's on land.

Oh, friend, no. The text says the commotion "…will make the cities of Judah a desolation, a haunt for jackals." (Jeremiah 10:22) Full and thriving is the opposite of what's said. Desolation and jackals do not sound thriving to me.
Right, no thriving here. The commotion "…will make the cities of Judah a desolation, a haunt for jackals." (Jeremiah 10:22) Desolation is the word. Jackals are the ones who haunt those cities.

True, and it's a big one. The speaker says to the LORD, "I know, O LORD, that a man’s way is not his own; no one who walks directs his own steps." (Jeremiah 10:23) That's a humble thing to say out loud.

This one is true, friend. The speaker tells the LORD, "I know, O LORD, that a man’s way is not his own; no one who walks directs his own steps." (Jeremiah 10:23) It sounds like a hard line, but it's right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: Only with justice and not in anger
explanations.explanation: That's the request. The prayer says, "Correct me, O LORD, but only with justice—not in Your anger…" (Jeremiah 10:24) Asking for correction is brave. I'd be hiding behind the oven.

explanations.answer: Quickly so that it will soon be over
explanations.explanation: I get the hope, baker. Nobody likes a long correction. But the prayer says, "Correct me, O LORD, but only with justice—not in Your anger…" (Jeremiah 10:24) It's about how, not how fast.

explanations.answer: Privately and away from the people
explanations.explanation: Private feedback is nice, friend, but that's not what's asked. The prayer says, "Correct me, O LORD, but only with justice—not in Your anger…" (Jeremiah 10:24) Justice and no anger, that's the ask.

That's the word. The prayer says, "Correct me, O LORD, but only with justice—not in Your anger, or You will bring me to nothing." (Jeremiah 10:24) The prayer asks for correction with justice, and nothing is where anger would lead. I think that's a careful way to ask.
Repentance sounds like a fine ending, baker, but it's not in the verse. The prayer says, "…or You will bring me to nothing." (Jeremiah 10:24) The word is nothing.
Safety would be a happy ending, but the prayer says otherwise. Anger would "…bring me to nothing." (Jeremiah 10:24) That's exactly why correction is asked for with justice.
Wrath is right. The prayer says, "Pour out Your wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge You…" (Jeremiah 10:25) It's a heavy line, and the text doesn't soften it.
Mercy is a good word, but it's not what the prayer asks for here. It says, "Pour out Your wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge You…" (Jeremiah 10:25) The word is wrath, plain as that.

That would be a very different prayer, friend. The text says, "Pour out Your wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge You, and on the families that do not call on Your name." (Jeremiah 10:25) Wrath is the word.

That's the reason the prayer gives. "For they have devoured Jacob; they have consumed him and finished him off; they have devastated his homeland." (Jeremiah 10:25) Jacob here stands for God's people. It's a heavy ending, and the text gives it straight.

It's a thoughtful guess, baker, but the verse never says it. The reason given is, "For they have devoured Jacob; they have consumed him and finished him off…" (Jeremiah 10:25) Mocking prophets isn't in that line.

A treaty makes a neat reason, but the text doesn't mention one. It says, "For they have devoured Jacob; they have consumed him and finished him off; they have devastated his homeland." (Jeremiah 10:25) That's the reason it gives.
